items.setupText: Mina has a new job at a hotel. She starts on Monday.
items.taskText: What does Mina have?
options: a room she has booked
a holiday she has planned
a visit to meet a friend
work she will be paid to do
items.answer: work she will be paid to do
items.explanation: A job here is paid work at the hotel.

rationales.a room she has booked: A guest books a room; a job is work, not accommodation.
rationales.work she will be paid to do: A job here is paid work at the hotel.
rationales.a holiday she has planned: Starting a job means starting work, not taking a holiday.
rationales.a visit to meet a friend: A social visit is not a job.

findings: Job was paired with unrelated person and payment definitions.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates employment from being a hotel guest.
audit.levelReason: Short present-tense statements and familiar work suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Employment itself, not job applications.

items.setupText: 'My boss is Ana,' says a cook at the restaurant.
items.taskText: Who is Ana in relation to the cook?
options: a person who eats there
a person who delivers food
a person in charge of the cook's work
a person who works under the cook
items.answer: a person in charge of the cook's work
items.explanation: Your boss is the person you work under.

rationales.a person who eats there: A person eating there is a customer, not necessarily the cook's boss.
rationales.a person who delivers food: Delivery work does not make someone the cook's boss.
rationales.a person who works under the cook: That reverses the relationship: the boss directs the cook's work.
rationales.a person in charge of the cook's work: Your boss is the person you work under.

findings: Clinic wrapper added nothing; distractors mixed people, actions and periods.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies who directs whose work.
audit.levelReason: A familiar workplace role supports beginner comprehension.
audit.similarityNote: Direction of authority in a kitchen.

items.setupText: The garage will pay Luis for his work on Friday.
items.taskText: What will the garage do?
options: give Luis money
ask Luis for money
give Luis another job
ask Luis to take a rest
items.answer: give Luis money
items.explanation: 'Pay someone for work' means give that person money for doing it.

rationales.give Luis money: 'Pay someone for work' means give that person money for doing it.
rationales.ask Luis for money: That reverses the payment: the garage is paying Luis.
rationales.give Luis another job: Payment rewards work; it does not mean assigning more work.
rationales.ask Luis to take a rest: A rest is a break, not payment.

findings: The discussion tail was unnatural and the foils were unrelated nouns.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Follows who gives and who receives money.
audit.levelReason: A simple future work arrangement suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: Employer payment rather than customer purchasing.

items.setupText: A museum door says 'Staff only.'
items.taskText: Who is this entrance for?
options: people visiting the museum
people buying tickets
people waiting for a tour
people who work at the museum
items.answer: people who work at the museum
items.explanation: Staff are the people employed to work in an organization.

rationales.people visiting the museum: Visitors are not staff simply because they enter the museum.
rationales.people buying tickets: Buying admission makes someone a visitor, not a staff member.
rationales.people who work at the museum: Staff are the people employed to work in an organization.
rationales.people waiting for a tour: Tour groups are visitors; this entrance is for workers.

findings: The example wrapper and mixed-category definitions supplied no useful contrast.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets a common workplace entrance label.
audit.levelReason: A two-word sign with familiar roles suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: A group label on a museum door.

items.setupText: Omar's shift at the bakery is from six until two.
items.taskText: What do these times describe?
options: when Omar travels to work
when Omar is scheduled to work
when Omar takes his lunch break
when Omar buys his groceries
items.answer: when Omar is scheduled to work
items.explanation: A shift is a set period during which someone works.

rationales.when Omar travels to work: The journey is separate from his scheduled work period.
rationales.when Omar is scheduled to work: A shift is a set period during which someone works.
rationales.when Omar takes his lunch break: A break is a pause within work, not the whole shift.
rationales.when Omar buys his groceries: A work shift does not describe personal shopping.

findings: Worksheet framing left shift opposed to places and people.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Reads starting and finishing times for work.
audit.levelReason: Concrete clock times support A1 vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Whole work period, not the break item.

items.setupText: 'The keys are in my office, beside my computer,' says the school manager.
items.taskText: Where should you look?
options: in the room where meals are cooked
in the room where visitors sleep
in the room where the manager works
in the room where cars are kept
items.answer: in the room where the manager works
items.explanation: An office is a room or place used for work such as administration.

rationales.in the room where the manager works: An office is a room or place used for work such as administration.
rationales.in the room where meals are cooked: That is a kitchen; office does not name a cooking room.
rationales.in the room where visitors sleep: That is a guest room, not the manager's office.
rationales.in the room where cars are kept: A garage holds cars; an office is used for other work.

findings: Teacher-example wrapper and unrelated definitions made the decision trivial.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Locates an item from a basic workplace direction.
audit.levelReason: Familiar rooms and objects keep the demand at A1.
audit.similarityNote: Location within a school, not business opening hours.

items.setupText: A factory needs three more workers to pack boxes.
items.taskText: What does it need?
options: three more people to do the packing
three more people to buy the boxes
three more people to visit the factory
three more people to inspect a purchase
items.answer: three more people to do the packing
items.explanation: A worker is a person doing work; the sentence specifies packing.

rationales.three more people to buy the boxes: Buyers are customers; workers do the packing.
rationales.three more people to visit the factory: Visitors need not do the factory's work.
rationales.three more people to inspect a purchase: Inspecting a purchase is not the packing role described.
rationales.three more people to do the packing: A worker is a person doing work; the sentence specifies packing.

findings: Worker was tested against periods and tasks rather than plausible people.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies participants who perform the work.
audit.levelReason: A concrete factory activity suits beginner vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Staffing a manual task rather than naming a boss.

items.setupText: Our team has a meeting about the new menu at ten.
items.taskText: What will the team do at ten?
options: stop work to eat their own meals
serve the first customers
come together to discuss the menu
leave the restaurant for the day
items.answer: come together to discuss the menu
items.explanation: A meeting brings people together for discussion or shared business.

rationales.stop work to eat their own meals: A meeting about a menu is a discussion, not necessarily a meal.
rationales.serve the first customers: Serving customers is different from meeting to discuss work.
rationales.come together to discuss the menu: A meeting brings people together for discussion or shared business.
rationales.leave the restaurant for the day: A meeting is an activity at work, not the end of the working day.

findings: Report wrapper and person distractor did not test meeting meaning in use.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Understands a routine team calendar event.
audit.levelReason: One purpose and one time suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Restaurant planning, not appointment booking.

items.setupText: We take a ten-minute break at eleven, then return to work.
items.taskText: What happens during the break?
options: We finish our jobs for the day.
We stop working for a short time.
We begin a different job.
We work faster than before.
items.answer: We stop working for a short time.
items.explanation: A break is a temporary pause, followed here by returning to work.

A break is a temporary pause, followed here by returning to work.
They return after ten minutes; the working day is not over.
A break pauses work rather than changing the task.
Working faster is still working, not taking a break.

findings: Reception tail did not support the meaning; foils were unrelated definitions.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a pause from the end of a workday.
audit.levelReason: A short chronological sequence suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: Rest within a shift.

items.setupText: 'Your first task is to put labels on these jars.'
items.taskText: What does 'task' mean here?
options: the piece of work you must do
the person you work for
the place where you work
the time you can go home
items.answer: the piece of work you must do
items.explanation: Putting labels on jars is a particular task within the job.

rationales.the person you work for: A task is work to do, not the person assigning it.
rationales.the place where you work: The jars may be at a workstation, but task names the activity.
rationales.the time you can go home: A finishing time is not a task.
rationales.the piece of work you must do: Putting labels on jars is a particular task within the job.

findings: Calling a task easy provided no concrete example of one.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects an assigned task with the required action.
audit.levelReason: A direct instruction about objects suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: A piece of work within a job, not the whole job.

items.setupText: The hotel wants to meet Eva and ask her about her work before giving her a job.
items.taskText: Eva is going for a job ___.
options: break
interview
shift
holiday
items.answer: interview
items.explanation: A job interview is a meeting where an employer asks an applicant questions.

rationales.break: A break pauses work; this meeting is part of applying for work.
rationales.interview: A job interview is a meeting where an employer asks an applicant questions.
rationales.shift: A shift is scheduled work after someone has the job.
rationales.holiday: A holiday is time off, not a meeting to discuss getting a job.

findings: Manager repeated the boss item with another generic person definition.
audit.microSkill: Job interview as an employment meeting
audit.pedagogicalValue: Names an early stage in getting work.
audit.levelReason: A concrete explanation supports the useful A1 phrase job interview.
audit.similarityNote: Adds recruitment foundations instead of repeating boss.

items.setupText: Ben repairs shoes. A customer brings him a broken boot.
items.taskText: Who is the customer?
options: the person who teaches Ben repairs
the person who works for Ben
the person who sells tools to Ben
the person using Ben's repair service
items.answer: the person using Ben's repair service
items.explanation: A customer buys goods or uses a business's services, such as shoe repair.

rationales.the person who teaches Ben repairs: A teacher may train Ben, but customer names the person using his service.
rationales.the person who works for Ben: An employee works for him; a customer brings work to his business.
rationales.the person using Ben's repair service: A customer buys goods or uses a business's services, such as shoe repair.
rationales.the person who sells tools to Ben: That person supplies Ben; the customer here brings a boot for repair.

findings: Lesson tail and object distractors avoided the customer-role distinction.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends customer beyond buying goods in shops.
audit.levelReason: A familiar service and clear roles suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Service user, distinct from museum staff.

items.setupText: I work in the cleaning team at the airport.
items.taskText: What does 'team' name?
options: the list of things I need to clean
the building where I keep my tools
the group I work with
the hours when I do the cleaning
items.answer: the group I work with
items.explanation: A team is a group working together toward a shared purpose.

rationales.the list of things I need to clean: A list of tasks is not the people doing them.
rationales.the building where I keep my tools: A team is people, not their storage place.
rationales.the hours when I do the cleaning: Work hours describe a shift, not a team.
rationales.the group I work with: A team is a group working together toward a shared purpose.

findings: Small-team sentence used desk, phone and file as unrelated foils.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes membership of a shared work group.
audit.levelReason: A simple first-person workplace statement suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: A smaller working group rather than all staff.

items.setupText: Please put the papers on my desk, beside the keyboard.
items.taskText: Which object is the desk?
options: the chair I sit on
the cupboard I hang clothes in
the bag I carry to work
the table I use for work
items.answer: the table I use for work
items.explanation: A desk is a worktable, often holding papers or a computer.

rationales.the table I use for work: A desk is a worktable, often holding papers or a computer.
rationales.the chair I sit on: The chair is a seat; the desk is the work surface.
rationales.the cupboard I hang clothes in: A cupboard stores things; desk names the table here.
rationales.the bag I carry to work: A bag may carry papers, but it is not a desk.

findings: Notice-board wrapper paired furniture with documents and devices.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Understands a common instruction about a work surface.
audit.levelReason: Concrete furniture supports A1 comprehension.
audit.similarityNote: Furniture, not a room or document.

items.setupText: 'Please phone the driver. Do not send a text.'
items.taskText: What should you do?
options: speak to the driver in a call
write the driver a short message
write down the driver's number
wait for the driver to call you
items.answer: speak to the driver in a call
items.explanation: 'Phone' is a verb here: make a telephone call to someone.

rationales.write the driver a short message: The instruction explicitly asks for a call instead of a text.
rationales.speak to the driver in a call: 'Phone' is a verb here: make a telephone call to someone.
rationales.write down the driver's number: Recording a number does not contact the driver.
rationales.wait for the driver to call you: The instruction asks you to make the call.

findings: Ringing-phone definition had no contrast with other communication actions.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Turns a work instruction into the correct contact method.
audit.levelReason: A common verb in a short instruction suits A1.
audit.similarityNote: Voice contact rather than the email-message item.

items.setupText: The blue file contains all the papers about the kitchen repairs.
items.taskText: What is kept in this file?
options: documents about the repair work
tools for repairing the kitchen
food for the kitchen staff
money to pay the repair workers
items.answer: documents about the repair work
items.explanation: A paper file keeps related documents together.

rationales.tools for repairing the kitchen: Tools do the repairs; this file holds information about them.
rationales.food for the kitchen staff: The file is for papers, not food storage.
rationales.documents about the repair work: A paper file keeps related documents together.
rationales.money to pay the repair workers: Bills may be filed, but a file is not the payment itself.

findings: Drawer context used sales and shop definitions as irrelevant alternatives.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects a paper file to related work records.
audit.levelReason: Physical papers keep this file meaning accessible at A1.
audit.similarityNote: Stored records, not a blank form.

items.setupText: On your first day, you receive a form with spaces for your name and address.
items.taskText: What should you do to complete the form?
options: write a story about your first day
draw a map of the building
give the requested information
make a list of questions for your boss
items.answer: give the requested information
items.explanation: To complete this form, fill its spaces with the information requested.

rationales.give the requested information: To complete this form, fill its spaces with the information requested.
rationales.write a story about your first day: A form asks for particular details, not a free-form story.
rationales.draw a map of the building: The spaces request a name and address, not a building map.
rationales.make a list of questions for your boss: Your questions do not complete the requested personal details.

findings: Tutor wrapper did not show how a form is used.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Understands what filling in a form requires.
audit.levelReason: Name and address are familiar A1 information.
audit.similarityNote: Supplying information rather than storing records.

items.setupText: 'Our summer sale ends today. Tomorrow these shirts go back to their usual prices.'
items.taskText: What does 'sale' mean in this notice?
options: a day when the shop is closed
a time when goods cost less than usual
a delivery of new shirts
a change in the shop's owner
items.answer: a time when goods cost less than usual
items.explanation: A sale can mean a period of reduced prices, as the return to usual prices shows.

rationales.a day when the shop is closed: The shop is selling shirts; sale does not mean closure.
rationales.a delivery of new shirts: A delivery brings stock; the notice concerns prices.
rationales.a change in the shop's owner: Nothing here concerns ownership of the business.
rationales.a time when goods cost less than usual: A sale can mean a period of reduced prices, as the return to usual prices shows.

findings: The sale-ended sentence likely meant a discount event, but the key gave only an act of selling.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Disambiguates a common retail notice.
audit.levelReason: Everyday prices and a short notice suit A1.
audit.similarityNote: Retail pricing rather than an individual purchase.

items.setupText: I work part-time at a bookshop: just two afternoons a week.
items.taskText: What does 'part-time' tell you?
options: I work there for no money.
I work fewer hours than a full-time worker.
I work in two different shops.
I work there only while travelling.
items.answer: I work fewer hours than a full-time worker.
items.explanation: Part-time work uses only part of the usual full working week.

'Part-time' describes working hours, not whether the work is paid.
rationales.I work fewer hours than a full-time work: Part-time work uses only part of the usual full working week.
Two afternoons do not mean two employers; 'part-time' concerns hours.
'Part-time' does not describe a travel arrangement.

findings: Shop definition repeated the everyday location pattern without a work distinction.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Reads a basic description of working hours.
audit.levelReason: Two afternoons gives concrete support for the A1 foundation.
audit.similarityNote: Weekly working pattern, not a single shift.

items.setupText: 'I sent you an email with tomorrow's room number.'
items.taskText: Where should you look for the room number?
options: on a paper notice by the door
in a recorded phone message
on a printed envelope in the post
in your email messages
items.answer: in your email messages
items.explanation: An email is an electronic message sent to an email address.

rationales.on a paper notice by the door: A notice is not the email the speaker sent.
rationales.in a recorded phone message: An email is written electronic communication, not a voice recording.
rationales.in your email messages: An email is an electronic message sent to an email address.
rationales.on a printed envelope in the post: Postal mail is different from an email message.

findings: Class-website wrapper opposed an email to unrelated employment definitions.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Locates work information in the named message channel.
audit.levelReason: A short practical message suits beginner use.
audit.similarityNote: Receiving written information rather than making a call.

items.setupText: The deadline for sending your lunch order is 10 a.m.
items.taskText: Which action meets the deadline?
options: Send the order by ten.
Start choosing lunch at 10:15.
Send the order when lunch arrives.
Wait until ten before reading the menu.
items.answer: Send the order by ten.
items.explanation: A deadline is the latest time an action must be completed.

Starting after ten is already too late for this deadline.
Delivery happens after ordering; it does not meet the stated sending time.
A deadline is the latest time an action must be completed.
The order must be sent by ten, not merely considered then.

findings: Friday/form example used documents and people as unrelated foils.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes starting from completing an action on time.
audit.levelReason: One familiar order and time suit A2.
audit.similarityNote: Routine ordering deadline, not a general schedule.

items.setupText: After repairing our printer, the engineer emailed an invoice for $80.
items.taskText: What is this document for?
options: confirming that we have paid
offering us a new printer for $80
recording our request for a repair
telling us what we need to pay
items.answer: telling us what we need to pay
items.explanation: An invoice lists charges and requests payment; it is not itself proof of payment.

rationales.telling us what we need to pay: An invoice lists charges and requests payment; it is not itself proof of payment.
rationales.confirming that we have paid: A receipt normally confirms payment; an invoice requests it.
rationales.offering us a new printer for $80: This invoice charges for the completed repair, not a proposed new purchase.
rationales.recording our request for a repair: The request came before the work; this document gives the charge afterwards.

findings: Clinic sentence did not distinguish an invoice from other transaction documents.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes a request for payment.
audit.levelReason: A single completed repair supports A2 document vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Amount owed; receipt later tests payment evidence.

items.setupText: Nora checks the packing team's work each day. She is their supervisor.
items.taskText: Which description fits Nora's role?
options: She buys the boxes they pack.
She visits to learn about their jobs.
She oversees their day-to-day work.
She delivers supplies from another company.
items.answer: She oversees their day-to-day work.
items.explanation: A supervisor checks and directs the work of other people.

A buyer purchases goods; a supervisor oversees the work.
A visitor observing the work is not necessarily responsible for it.
rationales.She delivers supplies from another compa: A supplier provides materials, not day-to-day supervision.
A supervisor checks and directs the work of other people.

findings: Leaving-permission example opposed a person to times and activities.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects supervisory responsibility with oversight.
audit.levelReason: A concrete daily duty supports the A2 role word.
audit.similarityNote: Ongoing checking, not simply identifying one's boss.

items.setupText: The careers adviser can see me at three. I have an appointment with her.
items.taskText: What has been arranged?
options: a job she has already offered me
a time for us to meet
a class that anyone can join
a deadline for paying her
items.answer: a time for us to meet
items.explanation: An appointment is an agreed meeting at a particular time.

rationales.a job she has already offered me: An appointment to meet is not a job offer.
rationales.a time for us to meet: An appointment is an agreed meeting at a particular time.
rationales.a class that anyone can join: This appointment is arranged with the speaker, not an open class.
rationales.a deadline for paying her: A meeting time is not a payment deadline.

findings: Bare time statement gave no contrast between a meeting and other arrangements.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a meeting booking from its possible outcome.
audit.levelReason: Personal scheduling language suits A2.
audit.similarityNote: One-to-one careers advice, not team discussion.

items.setupText: My usual workday ends at five, but yesterday I worked overtime until seven.
items.taskText: What was different yesterday?
options: I arrived after my usual start time.
I took extra time off.
I did the same work more quickly.
I worked beyond my usual hours.
items.answer: I worked beyond my usual hours.
items.explanation: Overtime is work outside the normal working hours.

Overtime is work outside the normal working hours.
Arriving late is not what 'overtime' means; the sentence concerns extra hours at the end.
Time off is time not working, whereas overtime adds work.
'Overtime' describes additional working time, not speed.

findings: Worksheet sentence offered no baseline hours and used unrelated pay and training meanings.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes extra work from lateness or time off.
audit.levelReason: A simple usual/yesterday contrast suits A2.
audit.similarityNote: Extra daily hours, not part-time employment.

items.setupText: The work schedule now shows cleaning at eight and deliveries at nine.
items.taskText: What information does a schedule give?
options: when activities are planned to happen
how much each activity costs
how well each activity was done
why each activity was chosen
items.answer: when activities are planned to happen
items.explanation: A schedule sets out planned activities and their times.

rationales.how much each activity costs: Costs belong in a budget, not necessarily a schedule.
rationales.how well each activity was done: A schedule plans activities; it does not assess their quality.
rationales.when activities are planned to happen: A schedule sets out planned activities and their times.
rationales.why each activity was chosen: Reasons may be explained separately; a schedule primarily organizes timing.

findings: Changed-schedule example gave no actual scheduled content.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies the information in a work timetable.
audit.levelReason: Two concrete activities and times fit A2.
audit.similarityNote: Sequence of planned activities rather than latest submission time.

items.setupText: The job offers a salary of $30,000 a year, paid monthly.
items.taskText: What does the salary describe?
options: the money I must pay for training
the regular amount I earn from the job
the money customers spend at the business
the extra gift I receive at the end of the year
items.answer: the regular amount I earn from the job
items.explanation: Salary is regular pay for employment; an annual amount may be paid in monthly parts.

rationales.the money I must pay for training: A salary is paid to the worker, not charged to them.
rationales.the regular amount I earn from the job: Salary is regular pay for employment; an annual amount may be paid in monthly parts.
rationales.the money customers spend at the busines: Customer spending is business income, not the employee's salary.
rationales.the extra gift I receive at the end of t: An extra award is a bonus; salary is regular pay.

findings: Monthly-pay sentence had no relevant alternative types of money.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates regular earnings from bonuses and business income.
audit.levelReason: No calculation is needed; the concrete pay offer suits A2.
audit.similarityNote: Regular earnings, not payment direction alone.

items.setupText: Before using the new coffee machine, staff will have training.
items.taskText: What should staff expect?
options: a decision about who gets the job
instruction and practice in using it
a record of their monthly pay
a review of last year's sales
items.answer: instruction and practice in using it
items.explanation: Workplace training develops the knowledge and skills needed for a task.

rationales.a decision about who gets the job: Choosing new employees is recruitment; these staff are already employed.
rationales.a record of their monthly pay: A pay record is not training.
rationales.a review of last year's sales: A sales review examines results, not how to operate the new machine.
rationales.instruction and practice in using it: Workplace training develops the knowledge and skills needed for a task.

findings: New-staff example repeated its definition with receipt and employee foils.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects training with learning through instruction and practice.
audit.levelReason: Familiar equipment makes the work activity concrete at A2.
audit.similarityNote: Learning machine operation rather than general onboarding.

items.setupText: The museum employs Jo as a guide. Jo is an employee; the museum is her employer.
items.taskText: Which description of 'employer' is correct here?
options: the visitors Jo shows around
the person Jo works beside
the organization that gives Jo paid work
the guide who receives the pay
items.answer: the organization that gives Jo paid work
items.explanation: An employer employs someone; an employee works for that employer.

rationales.the visitors Jo shows around: The visitors use the museum's service but do not employ Jo.
rationales.the person Jo works beside: A fellow worker is a colleague, not necessarily an employer.
rationales.the organization that gives Jo paid work: An employer employs someone; an employee works for that employer.
rationales.the guide who receives the pay: Jo receives pay as the employee; the question asks about the employer.

findings: Employee/card example did not test the easily confused employer/employee relationship.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes the two sides of an employment relationship.
audit.levelReason: A named person and organization make the A2 contrast clear.
audit.similarityNote: Paired role words, not customer or supervisor roles.

items.setupText: A passenger cannot find her booking. The airline's customer service team helps her.
items.taskText: Which task belongs to customer service in this situation?
options: helping the passenger solve her booking problem
repairing the aircraft's engine
planning the pilots' work hours
choosing uniforms for employees
items.answer: helping the passenger solve her booking problem
items.explanation: Customer service assists people using a business's goods or services.

rationales.helping the passenger solve her booking: Customer service assists people using a business's goods or services.
rationales.repairing the aircraft's engine: That is technical maintenance, not assistance with this customer's booking.
rationales.planning the pilots' work hours: Staff scheduling is different from helping a passenger.
rationales.choosing uniforms for employees: Internal purchasing does not address the passenger's problem.

findings: Job-requires-customer-service wording was vague and its distractors were isolated definitions.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes customer-facing help from internal operations.
audit.levelReason: A familiar travel problem supports A2 meaning.
audit.similarityNote: Solving a booking problem, not just naming a customer.

items.setupText: I bought stamps for the office. Accounts asked for the receipt.
items.taskText: Which document do they want?
options: a list of stamps I might buy next week
a record showing what I paid for the stamps
a note asking the post office for a price
a form asking permission to buy stamps
items.answer: a record showing what I paid for the stamps
items.explanation: A receipt records a completed purchase and payment.

rationales.a list of stamps I might buy next week: A shopping list records intended purchases, not completed payment.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies who decides to end employment.

wrapping the goods for travel
bringing the parcel to the client

rationales.placing the order with a supplier: Ordering occurred before the courier collected the parcel.
rationales.wrapping the goods for travel: Packing prepares goods for transport; delivery is the later arrival.
rationales.bringing the parcel to the client: 'Deliver' means take something to its intended recipient or destination.

findings: Daily-package sentence allowed supply as a broad overlapping definition.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes the two ends of a courier journey.
audit.levelReason: A two-step everyday sequence suits A2.
audit.similarityNote: Business transport, not merely noticing parcel arrival.

items.setupText: The workshop will supply gloves, so participants do not need to bring their own.

options: ask participants to buy gloves elsewhere
provide gloves for participants to use
collect participants' gloves at the door
teach participants to make gloves

rationales.ask participants to buy gloves elsewhere: That conflicts with supplying gloves itself.
rationales.provide gloves for participants to use: 'Supply' means provide something needed; the sentence removes the need to bring gloves.
rationales.collect participants' gloves at the door: Collecting their gloves would take them in, not provide them.
rationales.teach participants to make gloves: Teaching a skill is different from providing the actual equipment.

findings: Office-notebooks wrapper used unrelated deadline and person definitions.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Understands what an organizer provides rather than what to bring.
audit.levelReason: A familiar practical item supports A2 instructions.
audit.similarityNote: Provision for a workshop, distinct from courier transport.

items.setupText: Before the designer starts, both sides sign a contract setting out the fee and the work to be done.

a record showing the designer has been paid
a message advertising the designer's services
a preliminary suggestion neither side has accepted
items.answer: an agreement setting out the parties' commitments

rationales.an agreement setting out the parties' co: A contract establishes agreed obligations, here the work and the fee.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies agreed commitments without defining all contracts as written.
audit.levelReason: Concrete service terms suit B1 document vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Agreed obligations, not general organizational policy.

rationales.The charity uses her professional servic: A client is a person or organization receiving a professional service.

rationales.The charity supplies her office equipmen: A supplier provides goods; this client receives accountancy services.

findings: Clinic refund wrapper offered rules and budgets instead of competing service roles.
audit.microSkill: Client as recipient of professional service
audit.pedagogicalValue: Tracks a service relationship between organizations and professionals.
audit.levelReason: A short accountancy scenario develops B1 role vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Professional client rather than retail customer.

items.setupText: The firm's travel policy says employees should book economy seats on work trips.

the organization's rule for travel arrangements
the list of flights available tomorrow
one employee's personal travel preference

rationales.the organization's rule for travel arran: A policy states an organization's approach or rules on a subject.
rationales.the ticket for one employee's next fligh: A ticket is a particular booking, not the general rule.
rationales.the list of flights available tomorrow: A timetable gives available journeys, not the firm's booking rules.
rationales.one employee's personal travel preferenc: The policy applies as the firm's rule, not merely as an individual's preference.

findings: Privacy-policy example lacked policy-versus-instance alternatives.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a general work rule from a particular booking.
audit.levelReason: Routine business travel suits B1.

items.setupText: Lena submitted her application for the library post yesterday; interviews are next week.

formally asked to be considered for the job

items.explanation: A job application is a formal request to be considered for employment.

rationales.formally asked to be considered for the: A job application is a formal request to be considered for employment.

findings: Signed-application example did not identify what was being requested.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes applying from being selected or starting work.

The venue has fewer than 600 seats.

rationales.Its cost exceeds the amount available fo: A budget sets spending resources or limits; this venue costs more than the entire allowance.

A colleague is someone you work with; identical duties are not required.
'Colleague' does not specify authority over the speaker.

the profit the business makes from the employee

audit.levelReason: Concrete delivery and quality problems fit B1.
audit.similarityNote: Customer dissatisfaction, not an employee grievance procedure.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes what to consult before ordering supplies.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets a common agreement between coworkers.

items.taskText: What has definitely increased?
options: the amount paid for each hour of work
my total pay for the week
the number of hours in each shift
the bonus for finishing early
items.answer: the amount paid for each hour of work
items.explanation: An hourly wage is the rate earned per hour, distinct from total earnings.

rationales.my total pay for the week: Fewer hours may offset the higher rate; total pay is not established.
rationales.the bonus for finishing early: An hourly wage is a regular rate, not a completion bonus.
rationales.the amount paid for each hour of work: An hourly wage is the rate earned per hour, distinct from total earnings.

findings: Increased-wage sentence offered no distinction between rate and total pay.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids assuming that a higher rate always means higher weekly pay.
audit.levelReason: A two-factor everyday work comparison suits B1.
audit.similarityNote: Rate of pay, not annual salary or extra benefits.

items.setupText: The supplier offered a discount for a larger order, and our buyer asked for a longer payment period. They are negotiating the terms.
items.taskText: Which description fits 'negotiating'?
options: announcing terms that the other side must accept
recording the details of an agreement already reached
checking whether a previous agreement was followed
discussing terms with the aim of reaching agreement
items.answer: discussing terms with the aim of reaching agreement
items.explanation: Negotiating involves exchanges intended to find mutually acceptable terms; success is not guaranteed.

rationales.announcing terms that the other side mus: Negotiation involves seeking agreement, not merely imposing one side's terms.
rationales.recording the details of an agreement al: These exchanges concern reaching terms, not simply recording settled ones.
rationales.discussing terms with the aim of reachin: Negotiating involves exchanges intended to find mutually acceptable terms; success is not guaranteed.
rationales.checking whether a previous agreement wa: Checking compliance examines performance against existing terms rather than discussing new ones.

findings: Price sentence lacked evidence of negotiation and used unrelated process verbs.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes reciprocal discussion without assuming a completed deal.
audit.levelReason: Two negotiable terms support a B2 process distinction.
audit.similarityNote: Exchange of commercial terms rather than audience tone.

items.setupText: Finance has checked the figures, but the director still needs to authorize the payment.
items.taskText: What remains for the director to do?
options: give the necessary permission for it
calculate the total again
confirm that the supplier has received it
request the supplier's original price
items.answer: give the necessary permission for it
items.explanation: 'Authorize' means formally permit an action; checking figures does not itself supply approval.

rationales.give the necessary permission for it: 'Authorize' means formally permit an action; checking figures does not itself supply approval.
rationales.calculate the total again: Verification has happened; authorization is a different responsibility.
rationales.confirm that the supplier has received i: Receipt occurs after payment; the payment still needs permission.
rationales.request the supplier's original price: The figures already exist; authorization does not mean asking for a quotation.

findings: Manager-only example used inventory as a remote noun foil.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates approval authority from accounting checks and payment completion.
audit.levelReason: Several stages in a routine process suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: Permission stage, not negotiating the terms.

items.setupText: The new booking system has been designed and approved. The operations team will implement it next month.
items.taskText: What will the team do next month?
options: decide whether the idea is worth considering
put the approved system into operation
draw up the first proposal for it
assess last year's results from using it
items.answer: put the approved system into operation
items.explanation: 'Implement' means carry out a plan or put a system into practical use.

rationales.decide whether the idea is worth conside: Design and approval are complete; implementation is beyond initial consideration.
rationales.draw up the first proposal for it: A proposal precedes the approved design.
rationales.assess last year's results from using it: It has not yet been put into use, so that assessment is premature.
rationales.put the approved system into operation: 'Implement' means carry out a plan or put a system into practical use.

findings: During-discussion tail blurred planning and actual implementation.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes execution from proposing and assessing.
audit.levelReason: A staged organizational change suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: Putting a system into use rather than improving its steps.

items.setupText: I paid the taxi fare myself. The company will reimburse me after I submit the receipt.
items.taskText: What payment is being promised?
options: an advance before I incur the cost
repayment of my work-related expense
a refund from the taxi driver for poor service
an increase in my regular salary
items.answer: repayment of my work-related expense
items.explanation: 'Reimburse' means pay someone back for money they have spent.

rationales.an advance before I incur the cost: An advance precedes spending; the taxi fare has already been paid.
rationales.repayment of my work-related expense: 'Reimburse' means pay someone back for money they have spent.
rationales.a refund from the taxi driver for poor s: The company, not the taxi driver, will repay this expense.
rationales.an increase in my regular salary: Reimbursement covers a specific cost, not a new rate of pay.

findings: Travel-cost example did not contrast reimbursement with advances or refunds.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies who repays a work expense and when.
audit.levelReason: Related payment types form a B2 distinction.
audit.similarityNote: Employee expense recovery, not returning purchased goods.

items.setupText: Orders kept arriving while the packing line was closed. By Monday, the warehouse had a backlog.
items.taskText: What had accumulated?
options: goods rejected by customers
extra materials kept for future use
orders still waiting to be dealt with
records of orders already dispatched
items.answer: orders still waiting to be dealt with
items.explanation: A backlog is work that has accumulated because it has not yet been completed.

rationales.goods rejected by customers: A backlog need not consist of returned or rejected goods.
rationales.extra materials kept for future use: Reserve stock is not the outstanding work implied here.
rationales.orders still waiting to be dealt with: A backlog is work that has accumulated because it has not yet been completed.
rationales.records of orders already dispatched: Completed-order records are not work still waiting for attention.

findings: Inventory repeated B1's store-checks-inventory meaning with verb distractors.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes unfinished demand from stock and completed records.
audit.levelReason: A cause-and-accumulation scenario suits B2 operations vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Pending workload replaces the repeated inventory definition.

items.setupText: The project has allocated two technicians to testing, but testing will not begin until Thursday.
items.taskText: What has already happened?
options: The technicians have finished testing.
The project has recruited two new employees.
The testing work has been removed from the plan.
Resources have been assigned to a purpose.
items.answer: Resources have been assigned to a purpose.
items.explanation: 'Allocate' means assign resources for a particular use; the work may begin later.

rationales.Resources have been assigned to a purpos: 'Allocate' means assign resources for a particular use; the work may begin later.
Assigning people does not mean the task is completed.
rationales.The project has recruited two new employ: The technicians may already work there; allocation does not imply recruitment.
rationales.The testing work has been removed from t: Resources have been assigned to testing, not withdrawn from it.

findings: Training-funds example reduced allocation to vague giving.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes assignment of people as well as money.
audit.levelReason: Resource planning and later execution suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: Assigning capacity, not granting permission or spending cash.

items.setupText: The manager delegated preparation of the monthly rota to Priya, who already works on her team.
items.taskText: Which action did the manager take?
options: She entrusted a task to another team member.
She asked another company to run staffing.
She checked Priya's completed rota.
She gave Priya a permanent promotion.
items.answer: She entrusted a task to another team member.
items.explanation: 'Delegate' means give someone responsibility for carrying out a task.

rationales.She asked another company to run staffin: Priya is on the team; external contracting would be outsourcing.
Delegating assigns the preparation; it does not describe reviewing finished work.
Receiving a task does not itself change Priya's job level.
rationales.She entrusted a task to another team mem: 'Delegate' means give someone responsibility for carrying out a task.

findings: Delegated-the-report wording did not identify the actual task or recipient.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates task assignment from outsourcing and promotion.
audit.levelReason: Close organizational actions suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: Responsibility for preparation rather than staffing allocation.

items.setupText: The hotel evaluated three laundry services against cost, reliability and cleaning quality.
items.taskText: Which activity does 'evaluated' describe?
options: rewriting the services' offers
agreeing to purchase all three services
assessing how well the services met relevant criteria
advertising the services to guests
items.answer: assessing how well the services met relevant criteria
items.explanation: 'Evaluate' means judge quality or value against relevant considerations.

rationales.rewriting the services' offers: Evaluation judges offers; it need not alter their wording.
rationales.assessing how well the services met rele: 'Evaluate' means judge quality or value against relevant considerations.
rationales.agreeing to purchase all three services: Evaluation precedes or informs a choice; it is not acceptance of every option.
rationales.advertising the services to guests: Promotion publicizes a service rather than assessing it for purchase.

findings: Bare proposal example had no stated basis for evaluation.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes assessment from modification, selection and publicity.
audit.levelReason: Multiple work-relevant criteria suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: Supplier assessment rather than employee performance review.

items.setupText: The office streamlined expense claims by replacing three forms with one and removing a repeated approval step.
items.taskText: What is the central meaning of 'streamlined'?
options: moved all decisions to an outside provider
increased the number of checks for each claim
made the process simpler and more efficient
introduced a computer without changing the procedure
items.answer: made the process simpler and more efficient
items.explanation: Streamlining removes unnecessary complexity to improve how a process works.

rationales.made the process simpler and more effici: Streamlining removes unnecessary complexity to improve how a process works.
rationales.moved all decisions to an outside provid: The changes concern internal steps, not necessarily outsourcing.
rationales.increased the number of checks for each: An approval step was removed; streamlining here reduces duplication.
rationales.introduced a computer without changing t: No computer is mentioned, and the procedure itself changed.

findings: Registration example gave no evidence of simplification and used turnover as a foil.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes process simplification without assuming new technology.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting specific process changes suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: Removing duplicate steps rather than implementing a whole new system.

items.setupText: The theater outsourced its cleaning to a local firm while keeping ticket sales in-house.
items.taskText: Which contrast does 'outsourced' establish?
options: An outside provider does the cleaning; theater staff handle ticket sales.
Cleaning moved abroad; ticket sales stayed local.
Cleaning stopped; ticket sales continued.
Cleaners changed shifts; ticket sellers kept theirs.
items.answer: An outside provider does the cleaning; theater staff handle ticket sales.
items.explanation: Outsourcing gives work to an external provider, whereas in-house work is done within the organization.

rationales.Cleaning moved abroad; ticket sales stay: The cleaning firm is local; outsourcing concerns organizational boundaries, not national borders.
rationales.Cleaning stopped; ticket sales continued: Cleaning continues through a provider rather than ending.
rationales.An outside provider does the cleaning; t: Outsourcing gives work to an external provider, whereas in-house work is done within the organization.
rationales.Cleaners changed shifts; ticket sellers: The contrast concerns who provides the service, not shift times.

findings: Payroll example omitted the common outsourcing/offshoring confusion.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates external provision from moving work overseas.
audit.levelReason: A two-part organizational contrast suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: External service boundary rather than internal delegation.

items.setupText: The studio is trying to retain experienced animators by offering clearer career paths.
items.taskText: What is its main staffing aim?
options: attracting applicants who have never worked there
replacing experienced animators with trainees
reducing every animator's working hours
encouraging current animators to stay
items.answer: encouraging current animators to stay
items.explanation: 'Retain staff' means keep existing employees in the organization.

rationales.attracting applicants who have never wor: Recruiting new people is different from retaining existing employees.
rationales.encouraging current animators to stay: 'Retain staff' means keep existing employees in the organization.
rationales.replacing experienced animators with tra: Replacement loses the staff the studio wants to retain.
rationales.reducing every animator's working hours: Career paths may involve several measures, but 'retain' does not mean shorten hours.

findings: Benefits sentence used rule-following and quota definitions rather than staffing aims.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes keeping existing expertise as a staffing goal.
audit.levelReason: A work policy linked to staff behavior fits B2.
audit.similarityNote: Maintaining employees, not hiring assistants.

items.setupText: The report attributes frequent recruitment campaigns to high staff turnover.
items.taskText: What problem does 'staff turnover' name?
options: Employees spend too much time serving each customer.
Employees leave and need replacing frequently.
Employees generate unusually high sales.
Employees work rotating morning and evening shifts.
items.answer: Employees leave and need replacing frequently.
items.explanation: 'Staff turnover' describes the rate of departures and replacement within a workforce.

rationales.Employees spend too much time serving ea: Service time is not the staffing movement called turnover.
'Turnover' can refer to business sales, but 'staff turnover' concerns employees leaving and being replaced.
rationales.Employees work rotating morning and even: Shift rotation is a schedule pattern, not staff turnover.
rationales.Employees leave and need replacing frequ: 'Staff turnover' describes the rate of departures and replacement within a workforce.

findings: Unqualified turnover allowed a sales sense; wage timing did not resolve it securely.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses the modifier staff to select the relevant business sense.
audit.levelReason: Business polysemy and a recruitment consequence suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: Workforce movement, not shift changes or sales income.

items.setupText: From sixty applications, the panel shortlisted five people for the final interviews.
items.taskText: What is true of those five at this stage?
options: They have all been offered permanent jobs.
They have withdrawn from the process.
They remain under consideration after an initial selection.
They have been placed in a final order of preference.
items.answer: They remain under consideration after an initial selection.
items.explanation: A shortlist contains the candidates selected for further consideration, not necessarily the eventual appointee.

rationales.They remain under consideration after an: A shortlist contains the candidates selected for further consideration, not necessarily the eventual appointee.
rationales.They have all been offered permanent job: Final interviews are still to come; shortlisting is not appointment.
Shortlisted people continue in the process rather than leave it.
rationales.They have been placed in a final order o: A shortlist need not rank its members.

findings: Shortlisted-five sentence gave a broad group gloss without testing selection stage.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes preliminary selection from an offer or ranked result.
audit.levelReason: Close recruitment outcomes suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: Advancement within selection, beyond the B1 candidate label.

items.setupText: The inspection checked compliance with the warehouse's own labeling procedure.
items.taskText: What did the inspectors examine?
options: whether workers personally liked the procedure
whether a new labeling method could be invented
whether the labels were selling profitably
whether the required labeling steps were being followed
items.answer: whether the required labeling steps were being followed
items.explanation: 'Compliance' means acting in accordance with specified rules or requirements.

rationales.whether workers personally liked the pro: Compliance concerns following requirements, not agreeing with them.
rationales.whether a new labeling method could be i: Designing a method differs from checking adherence to an existing one.
rationales.whether the required labeling steps were: 'Compliance' means acting in accordance with specified rules or requirements.
rationales.whether the labels were selling profitab: Labeling compliance is unrelated to selling labels for profit.

findings: Notice-board audit example omitted which requirements were being checked.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates following requirements from approving of or designing them.
audit.levelReason: A concrete inspection supports B2 organizational vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Adherence to internal requirements, without legal knowledge.

items.setupText: Each sales representative has a monthly quota of forty new subscriptions.
items.taskText: What does the quota specify here?
options: the price charged for each subscription
the sales amount each representative is expected to achieve
the number of customers who cancelled last month
the total number of representatives employed
items.answer: the sales amount each representative is expected to achieve
items.explanation: A sales quota is a specified target quantity for a period.

rationales.the price charged for each subscription: Forty is the required number of sales, not a price.
rationales.the number of customers who cancelled la: Cancellations are past results, not this target for new subscriptions.
rationales.the total number of representatives empl: The quota applies to each representative; it does not count staff.
rationales.the sales amount each representative is: A sales quota is a specified target quantity for a period.

findings: Met-quota sentence gave no quantity or period and used role definitions as foils.
audit.microSkill: Sales quota as an assigned target
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes required output from price and recorded results.
audit.levelReason: A quantified work target suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: Expected sales quantity rather than pay or available budget.

items.setupText: The museum asked each vendor bidding to supply display cases for a sample.
items.taskText: Who are the vendors in this sentence?
options: the museum's visitors judging the display
the museum employees approving the purchase
the people donating objects for the cases
the businesses offering to supply the cases
items.answer: the businesses offering to supply the cases
items.explanation: A vendor is a seller or supplier; here the vendors are prospective providers.

rationales.the museum's visitors judging the displa: Visitors are users of the museum, not suppliers bidding for work.
rationales.the businesses offering to supply the ca: A vendor is a seller or supplier; here the vendors are prospective providers.
rationales.the museum employees approving the purch: Buyers select suppliers; they are not the vendors in this relationship.
rationales.the people donating objects for the case: Donors contribute exhibits, not necessarily the cases being procured.

findings: Invoice sentence used liability and revenue meanings instead of related transaction roles.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies the selling side before a contract is awarded.
audit.levelReason: A bidding context develops B2 role precision.
audit.similarityNote: Prospective supply relationship, not a professional client.

items.setupText: Even in a quiet month, the studio still pays rent and insurance. These overheads put pressure on the business.
items.taskText: What does 'overheads' mean here?
options: the selling price of each completed design
ongoing costs of running the business
the profit left after expenses
the extra charge for a single rush order
items.answer: ongoing costs of running the business
items.explanation: Overheads are general operating costs, not costs tied solely to one particular job.

rationales.ongoing costs of running the business: Overheads are general operating costs, not costs tied solely to one particular job.
rationales.the selling price of each completed desi: Selling prices are income terms, not rent and insurance costs.
rationales.the profit left after expenses: Overheads are expenses to be paid, not the remaining profit.
rationales.the extra charge for a single rush order: A rush surcharge is linked to a specific order, unlike these ongoing costs.

findings: Bare liability definition was repeated at C1 and drifted into legal terminology.
audit.microSkill: Overheads versus job-specific charges and profit
audit.pedagogicalValue: Understands general operating-cost language in everyday business discussion.
audit.levelReason: Concrete rent and insurance examples support B2.
audit.similarityNote: Adds ongoing operating costs instead of repeated liability.

items.setupText: During onboarding, new employees receive system access, meet their teams and learn how the organization works.
items.taskText: What is the purpose of onboarding?
options: helping new employees become established in the organization
selecting which applicants should receive offers
reviewing whether long-serving staff should be promoted
transferring an entire service to an outside company
items.answer: helping new employees become established in the organization
items.explanation: Onboarding introduces new staff to the practical and social aspects of their roles.

rationales.selecting which applicants should receiv: Recruitment selects applicants; these people are already new employees.
rationales.reviewing whether long-serving staff sho: Onboarding supports entrants, not promotion reviews for established staff.
rationales.helping new employees become established: Onboarding introduces new staff to the practical and social aspects of their roles.
rationales.transferring an entire service to an out: That is outsourcing, not settling new employees into work.

findings: Begins-Monday example did not show onboarding's scope beyond a single introduction.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes practical access and social integration as parts of joining work.
audit.levelReason: A multi-part entry process suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: Joining an organization, distinct from training on one machine.

items.setupText: The cafe's sales revenue rose, but higher ingredient costs left it with less profit.
items.taskText: Which distinction explains how both statements can be true?
options: Revenue excludes sales to regular customers.
Profit is counted before the cafe pays its costs.
Revenue is sales income; profit allows for costs.
Revenue and profit name the same amount.
items.answer: Revenue is sales income; profit allows for costs.
items.explanation: Revenue measures income from sales here, whereas profit depends on costs as well.

rationales.Revenue excludes sales to regular custom: Sales revenue includes those sales; customer frequency is not the distinction.
rationales.Profit is counted before the cafe pays i: Profit is what remains after relevant costs, not before them.
The sentence contrasts sales income with what remains after costs.
rationales.Revenue is sales income; profit allows f: Revenue measures income from sales here, whereas profit depends on costs as well.

findings: Money-a-business-receives gloss was too broad and did not distinguish revenue from profit.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets different business results without treating all incoming money as profit.
audit.levelReason: A qualitative income/cost contrast suits B2 without accounting calculation.
audit.similarityNote: Business income result, distinct from staff turnover and pay.

items.setupText: 'Procurement has asked us to compare three quotes before ordering,' the office manager said.
items.taskText: Who or what does 'Procurement' refer to here?
options: the team responsible for obtaining goods and services
the goods that have already arrived
the customer waiting for the finished product
the payment sent to the chosen supplier
items.answer: the team responsible for obtaining goods and services
items.explanation: A department's function can stand for its staff; 'Procurement' here means the buying team.

rationales.the goods that have already arrived: Goods cannot ask the manager to compare quotes.
rationales.the team responsible for obtaining goods: A department's function can stand for its staff; 'Procurement' here means the buying team.
rationales.the customer waiting for the finished pr: The quotation request comes from the organization's purchasing function.
rationales.the payment sent to the chosen supplier: A payment cannot issue the request, and selection has not yet occurred.

findings: Procurement-approved-order referred to a department, but the key named only the buying process.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes a business function used to name the people doing it.
audit.levelReason: Common workplace shorthand with contextual agency suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: Department used as actor, not merely a process definition.

items.setupText: The designers finish twenty labels a day, but the single reviewer can approve only five. The director calls approval the bottleneck.
items.taskText: What does 'bottleneck' identify?
options: the stage requiring the most expensive equipment
the task considered most important to customers
the stage producing the largest amount of completed work
the stage restricting overall throughput
items.answer: the stage restricting overall throughput
items.explanation: A bottleneck restricts overall throughput because work cannot pass through it quickly enough.

rationales.the stage requiring the most expensive e: Equipment cost is not the limiting factor described.
rationales.the stage restricting overall throughput: A bottleneck restricts overall throughput because work cannot pass through it quickly enough.
rationales.the task considered most important to cu: Importance is not the defining feature; the approval capacity limits output.
rationales.the stage producing the largest amount o: Design produces more, but approval constrains what can move onward.

findings: Compliance repeated the B2 meaning with another audit sentence.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes limiting capacity from importance or cost.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting connected work stages suits C1.
audit.similarityNote: Capacity constraint replaces a repeated compliance definition.

items.setupText: A supplier quotes a six-week lead time for custom desks, although making each desk takes only two days.
items.taskText: How can these statements be consistent?
options: Lead time measures how long the desks should last.
Lead time excludes the time before production starts.
It includes waiting as well as manufacture.
The quoted six weeks describes the desk's assembly labor alone.
items.answer: It includes waiting as well as manufacture.
items.explanation: Commercial lead time includes the time needed before an order can be fulfilled, which may extend beyond active production.

rationales.Lead time measures how long the desks sh: Expected useful life is different from the waiting period before supply.
rationales.Lead time excludes the time before produ: Lead time can include waiting for materials or a production slot.
rationales.The quoted six weeks describes the desk': The contrast with two days shows a broader order-to-fulfilment interval.
rationales.It includes waiting as well as manufactu: Commercial lead time includes the time needed before an order can be fulfilled, which may extend beyond active production.

findings: Procurement repeated B2's buying definition without advanced distinction.
audit.microSkill: Lead time versus active production time
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets a supplier's waiting period without equating it to labor time.
audit.levelReason: A distinction between elapsed and active work time suits C1.
audit.similarityNote: Supply timing rather than naming the purchasing team.

items.setupText: The design team's remit covers packaging, not the product recipe. It referred a proposed ingredient change to product development.
items.taskText: What does 'remit' delimit?
options: the matters the team is assigned to handle
the hours during which the team is available
the skills individual designers happen to possess
the amount the team has spent on packaging
items.answer: the matters the team is assigned to handle
items.explanation: A team's remit is its assigned area of responsibility or authority.

rationales.the matters the team is assigned to hand: A team's remit is its assigned area of responsibility or authority.
rationales.the hours during which the team is avail: Working hours concern availability, not the subject area assigned to the team.
rationales.the skills individual designers happen t: Someone may have skills beyond the team's remit; the term concerns assigned responsibility.
rationales.the amount the team has spent on packagi: Expenditure is not the boundary of responsibility named here.

findings: Contract/liability sentence repeated B2 and relied on a bare legal gloss.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes organizational responsibility without inferring personal incapacity.
audit.levelReason: Related boundaries of competence and assignment suit C1.
audit.similarityNote: Functional responsibility, not a legal-liability question.

items.setupText: Before changing delivery hours, the depot consulted drivers, neighboring residents and major customers as stakeholders.
items.taskText: Which description explains the residents' stakeholder status?
options: They have acquired an ownership share in the depot.
They have been given authority to decide the depot's hours.
They are parties to the depot's delivery contracts.
Their interests may be affected by the depot's decision.
items.answer: Their interests may be affected by the depot's decision.
items.explanation: Stakeholders have an interest in or are affected by an activity; ownership is not required.

rationales.They have acquired an ownership share in: Stakeholders need not be shareholders; consultation does not establish ownership.
rationales.They have been given authority to decide: Being affected and consulted does not establish decision-making authority.
rationales.Their interests may be affected by the d: Stakeholders have an interest in or are affected by an activity; ownership is not required.
rationales.They are parties to the depot's delivery: Residents can be stakeholders without being customers or contracting parties.

findings: Update-receipt example did not contrast stakeholder with shareholder.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes affected non-owners in organizational decisions.
audit.levelReason: Related institutional roles and a boundary distinction suit C1.
audit.similarityNote: Participation by affected groups, not endorsement or agreement.

items.setupText: The editor changed the workflow so illustrations reach the layout team before text is finalized. The number of assignments stayed the same.
items.taskText: What changed, rather than the workload?
options: the amount of work assigned to each employee
the range of benefits offered to the staff
the organization and passage of work between stages
the total number of publications commissioned
items.answer: the organization and passage of work between stages
items.explanation: Workflow concerns the organization and movement of work through stages.

rationales.the amount of work assigned to each empl: The sentence distinguishes organization of work from the amount of work.
rationales.the organization and passage of work bet: Workflow concerns the organization and movement of work through stages.
rationales.the range of benefits offered to the sta: Benefits concern employment conditions, not how illustrations reach layout.
rationales.the total number of publications commiss: Assignment numbers are unchanged; 'workflow' does not mean total commissioned output.

findings: Reduced-delays example equated workflow only with order and used payment foils.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates work organization from work volume.
audit.levelReason: Coordination between production stages suits C1.
audit.similarityNote: Information sequence, distinct from the capacity bottleneck.

items.setupText: A vacancy lists a full-time salary of $40,000, pro rata for part-time hours.
items.taskText: What does 'pro rata' tell a part-time applicant about the advertised figure?
options: The amount is adjusted in proportion to the hours worked.
It is the minimum regardless of hours worked.
It is paid only as a bonus after the first year.
It will be negotiated without reference to working hours.
items.answer: The amount is adjusted in proportion to the hours worked.
items.explanation: 'Pro rata' means in proportion; here the full-time figure is scaled to the agreed working hours.

rationales.It is the minimum regardless of hours wo: 'Pro rata' indicates proportional adjustment, not the same guaranteed amount for all hours.
rationales.It is paid only as a bonus after the fir: The phrase concerns proportion, not a performance bonus or waiting period.
rationales.It will be negotiated without reference: The advertisement explicitly links the proportion to part-time hours.
rationales.The amount is adjusted in proportion to: 'Pro rata' means in proportion; here the full-time figure is scaled to the agreed working hours.

findings: Remuneration reduced C1 to the already-tested basic meaning payment for work.
audit.microSkill: Pro rata in a salary advertisement

items.setupText: The publisher plans to reduce staffing through attrition rather than compulsory redundancies.

Employees keep their posts but work fewer hours.
Staff leave and their posts remain unfilled.
Departing employees are replaced by outside contractors.
items.answer: Staff leave and their posts remain unfilled.
items.explanation: Attrition reduces staff as people leave and their positions are not filled.

audit.microSkill: Attrition versus dismissal and reduced hours
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes mechanisms of workforce reduction.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting staffing changes through their mechanism suits C1.
audit.similarityNote: Non-replacement of departing staff, distinct from redundancy.

items.setupText: A British employer announced redundancies after closing its print room, while thanking the affected staff for their excellent work.
items.taskText: Which interpretation explains why the thanks and redundancies are compatible?
options: 'Redundancy' means a temporary break until printing restarts.
The jobs, not their performance, are the issue.
'Redundancy' means the employees chose to retire.
The employees are being promoted into more senior posts.
items.answer: The jobs, not their performance, are the issue.
items.explanation: In British employment usage, redundancy concerns jobs no longer required, not necessarily the workers' performance.

rationales.'Redundancy' means a temporary break unt: Redundancy concerns losing an unneeded job, not necessarily a temporary absence.

rationales.The jobs, not their performance, are the: In British employment usage, redundancy concerns jobs no longer required, not necessarily the workers' performance.
rationales.The employees are being promoted into mo: Redundancy is not a promotion, even when the employees' work is praised.

findings: Merger example lacked variety labeling and an employment-performance distinction.

items.setupText: After informal discussions failed, an employee lodged a grievance about how shift preferences had been allocated.
items.taskText: What change does 'lodged a grievance' signal?

The employee has accepted the allocation.
The employer has confirmed that the complaint is justified.
The employee has resigned from the organization.

rationales.The employee has submitted a formal comp: To lodge a grievance is to submit a formal workplace complaint.

rationales.The employee has resigned from the organ: A complaint can be pursued while the employee remains in the job.

findings: Reception-desk wrapper added no formal-versus-informal distinction.
audit.microSkill: Lodging a grievance versus resolving it
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates formal submission from a finding or resignation.
audit.levelReason: A change in procedural status suits C1 workplace reading.
audit.similarityNote: Employee complaint escalation through procedure, not customer dissatisfaction.

items.setupText: The project plan lists 'prototype accepted' as a milestone and 'a working prototype with instructions' as a deliverable.
items.taskText: What distinguishes the deliverable?
options: It is the amount of time the team expects to spend.
It is any event the team considers encouraging.
It is the specified output the team must provide.
It is the person responsible for approval.
items.answer: It is the specified output the team must provide.
items.explanation: A deliverable is an agreed product or result; a milestone marks a significant point or achievement.

rationales.It is the amount of time the team expect: Effort or duration is an input, not the product handed over.
rationales.It is any event the team considers encou: A deliverable is an agreed output, not simply a positive event.
rationales.It is the person responsible for approva: The approver is a role, whereas the deliverable is a result of work.
rationales.It is the specified output the team must: A deliverable is an agreed product or result; a milestone marks a significant point or achievement.

findings: Due-Friday sentence failed to distinguish the output from its deadline or milestone.

audit.levelReason: Interpreting adjacent project-plan categories suits C1.
audit.similarityNote: Work output, not a delivery parcel or submission time.

items.setupText: Unable to approve the requested exception herself, the coordinator escalated the issue to the operations director.
items.taskText: What does 'escalated' mean here?

referred it to someone with greater authority
increased the size of the requested exception
withdrew the issue from consideration
items.answer: referred it to someone with greater authority

rationales.referred it to someone with greater auth: In a workplace process, 'escalating an issue' can mean referring it to a higher decision-making level.
rationales.made the disagreement deliberately more: Escalate can describe worsening conflict, but this sentence identifies referral to a director.
rationales.increased the size of the requested exce: The requested exception is unchanged; its decision-maker changes.
